newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova votes, torn between East and West.
newsitem.headline: Moldova votes, torn between East and West.

text.p: Moldovans face harsh choices in a bitter presidential election on Sunday and the balance of forces shows the former Soviet republic is torn between East and West, between market reform and a big measure of state control.

At first sight, the two candidates in the second round run-off have much in common. Mircea Snegur, president since independence in 1991, and parliament speaker Petru Lucinschi were both leading Communist officials in Soviet days. Both hail from northern peasant stock, both are 56.
But the race has polarised the poor rural state of 4.3 million, sandwiched between Romania and Ukraine.

Snegur, backed by groups seeking closer ties with ethnic and linguistic kin in Romania, wants to plant the country firmly in the western camp. He promises free market reforms if he secures backing for constitutional change to strengthen the presidency.

Lucinschi, appealing to those who fear submersion in a greater Romania and who hanker for the better days of Soviet communism, says Chisinau must not turn its back on Moscow, which, among other things, supplies the bulk of its energy.

The speaker, openly backed by state television and much of the daily press, accuses Snegur of wanting to turn the largely honorific presidency into a "dictatorship", along the lines of President Alexander Lukashenko's controversial moves in Belarus.
Analysts say the two rivals are neck and neck after rallying support from the seven losers in the November 17 first round.
Mudslinging has marked the campaign as have warnings of potentially violent instability in a country which has seen civil war and a schism in the military in recent years.
Several hundred young people marched through Chisinau late on Wednesday calling for larger rallies in support of Snegur.

Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, a bitter foe of Snegur, says his government is ready to resign after the vote to "preserve civil peace". But he has asked the defence, security and interior ministers to tighten controls over their armed units.
The tall and bulky Snegur cultivates a "man of the people" image, bemoaning the hardships and misery of his nation and promising to dissolve the "corrupt" government and parliament.

An earlier attempt to take on the government, when Snegur tried to sack the defence minister for corruption, split the army in March. It ended when the Constitutional Court backed Sangheli and ruled Snegur out of order.
The president, who finished top in the first round with 39 percent of the vote, has not let up on the attack.
"We can no longer tolerate the rule of the monstrous coalition which has led the state and majority of people to bare subsistence," he said in a campaign radio broadcast.
"But all my efforts to change things to the better are blocked by revanchist communist forces grouping around Lucinschi," he added in a radio address on Wednesday.
The president has forged an alliance with pro-Bucharest nationalist Valeriu Matei who won nine percent on November 17.
Lucinschi, an intellectual who won 28 percent in the first round, has won the support of communist Vladimir Voronin, who polled 10 percent and Sangheli, who took nine percent.
Lucinschi presents himself as a moderate centre-leftist of the mould seen among many of eastern Europe's former communists.
"In civilised Europe, there is no state ruled by a tsar, but this is exactly where Mircea Snegur is heading in wishing to set up his autocracy," he told Chisinau businessmen recently.
The issue of ties to the West or East is painful in Moldova, carved by Stalin out of mostly Romanian territory in 1944.

The 700,000 mostly Slavic-speaking people east of the Dnestr river, along the Ukrainian border, broke away in 1990 for fear of being subsumed by Romania. Hundreds died in a 1992 civil war there, which was ended by the intervention of Russian troops.
